response.bodyText: {"rows":3,"os":0,"page":1,"total":25170,"documents":{"D735811":{"id":"735811","count":"Algeria","docty":"Internal Discussion Paper","owner":"Middle East and North Africa","entityids":{"entityid":"000009265_3960930181825"},"docdt":"1991-02-28T05:00:00Z","abstracts":{"cdata!":"This paper attempts to gauge the potential impact of full price liberalization on the general price level and future open inflation. First, the available evidence is evaluated to assess the degree of repressed inflation in Algeria and its potential impact on open inflation. The evaluation is based on a descriptive analysis of past macroeconomic policies, statistical comparison, and econometric analysis. Although there are clear indications that official prices are repressed in Algeria, the degree of repression and the impact of price liberalization on economic behavior are much less certain. Evaluation of the evidence suggests that, immediately lifting all remaining price controls would result in an immediate one-time jump in the general price level as measured by the official CPI. However, because the extent of parallel market activity is uncertain, the size of this increase and its impact on consumer behavior and future open inflation remain unclear. Given the uncertain impact of price liberalization, therefore, a flexible policy package is required for controlling inflation during the remainder of the transition. A tight medium-term monetary stance would be required if inflation accelerates and a more accommodating monetary stance preferred if precautionary measures taken to absorb liquidity and contain cost-push factors turn out to be deflationary."},"display_title":"Algeria : inflation in the transition","pdfurl":"http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/429831468913782253/pdf/Algeria-inflation-in-the-transition.pdf","txturl":"http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/429831468913782253/text/Algeria-inflation-in-the-transition.txt","guid":"429831468913782253","url":"http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/429831468913782253"},"D29882898":{"id":"29882898","count":"World","docty":"Policy Research Working Paper","entityids":{"entityid":"090224b085a7228f_1_0"},"docdt":"2018-05-10T04:00:00Z","abstracts":{"cdata!":"This paper presents a simple model with financial frictions where inflation increases the cost faced by firms holding liquid assets to hedge risky production against expenditure shocks. Inflation tilts firms' technology choice away from innovative activities and toward safer but return-dominated ones, and therefore reduces long-run growth. The theory makes specific predictions about how the severity of this adverse effect depends on industry characteristics. These predictions are tested with novel harmonized firm-level data from 139 developing countries, overcoming small sample problems constraining previous work. The analysis finds that inflation affects the composition but not the overall quantity of investment. A one percentage point increase in inflation reduces the establishment-level probability of innovation by 4.3 percent but does not affect total investment. Moreover, innovating firms display a stronger dependence on liquid assets, which, in turn, are negatively related to inflation. To make the simulation results instructive, the specific initial conditions chosen are those of the Polish economy, end of September 1992. The model and its simulations were used in Poland in 1992 in order to construct the 1993 budget, and may be used to discover the ratio of the budget deficit to Gross Domestic Product that is consistent with an inflation path acceptable to the policymaker.
